newsitem.title: DENMARK: Nordic justice ministers to meet on biker war.
newsitem.headline: Nordic justice ministers to meet on biker war.

text.p: Danish Justice Minister Bjoern Westh has invited Nordic colleagues to meet on Friday to plan joint action against rival motorcycle gangs who have turned one of Europe's most peaceful regions into a battlefield.
Danish and Swedish media said that Sweden's Laila Freivalds would attend the Copenhagen meeting, but on Monday night the Norwegian and Finnish justice ministers had yet to reply.

Denmark, shaken by an inter-gang anti-tank missile attack in the heart of Copenhagen on Sunday, expects an emergency bill to ban gang clubhouses from residential areas to become law by next weekend and is considering outlawing the gangs altogether, a justice ministry official told Reuters on Monday.
Sweden and Norway have said they will examine the bill in detail to see if they might usefully adopt it.

The bill, rushed to parliament last Friday, was a response to bomb, grenade and machine gun raids on biker clubs sited near family homes and it is likely to be followed by new police powers to tap phones and raid properties without a warrant.
"This isn't Denmark, this is war," Copenhagen police chief Hanne Bech Hansen told reporters after the shoulder-fired missile tore into a Hell's Angels' party at the gang's main city base on Sunday.

A man and woman died in the attack and 19 were wounded. Police on Monday night said that a 25-year-old man who had been in intensive care since the blast was now out of danger and was one of seven people remaining in hospital.

The raid was the bloodiest yet in months of escalating violence between the dominant Hell's Angels and the rival Bandidos. The clashes have left Danes and their Nordic neighbours wondering what became of their peaceful society.
"I simply don't understand it. It is not the Denmark I know," Westh said after the blast.

A batch of 12 Carl Gustav shoulder-fired, anti-tank missiles of the type used in the Copenhagen attack was stolen from Swedish army stores in 1994 near the port of Malmo, a brief ferry ride from Copenhagen.
Missiles identified as from the stolen batch were fired at two Hell's Angels' clubhouses in Denmark last April.
Conflict between the gangs, both local offshoots of U.S. groups with extensive European networks, began almost as soon as the Bandidos set up shop in the region in the summer of 1993.

In February 1994 a member of the Hell's Angels-affiliated Rednecks died in a gunfight after walking -- reportedly by accident -- into a Bandidos meeting at a night club in the Swedish port of Helsingborg.

The then newly elected president of the Bandidos, Mikael Ljunggren, was killed by a sniper as he rode his motorcycle north of the city in July 1995, in an ambush that investigators said could have been either a Hells Angels attack or the work of fellow gang members opposed to his leadership.
In March this year, attackers shot dead a Bandidos leader in the Finnish capital, Helsinki, and a Danish Bandido died in an ambush outside Copenhagen airport 10 days later.
A Danish Bandidos member was fatally shot in the head near the Norwegian city of Drammen in July.
